questions.stem: The principle of uniformitarianism states that:
options: Every rock layer contains the same fossils wherever it is found across the world
The processes that shape Earth today also operated in the past and can explain ancient rocks
Earth's rocks were all formed at the same time and have not changed since they formed
Rock layers are always deposited at the same uniform thickness everywhere on Earth
questions.explanation: Uniformitarianism holds that the physical and chemical processes we observe now, such as erosion, deposition and volcanism, also acted in the past. Geologists therefore interpret ancient rocks by comparing them with features forming today. It says nothing about layers having equal thickness or identical fossils.

questions.stem: A sandstone in a quarry shows ripple marks identical to those forming today on the sand of a tidal flat at Moreton Bay. Using uniformitarianism, what can be inferred?
options: The sandstone formed from sand moved by gently flowing water, such as in a shallow sea
The sandstone formed from lava that cooled quickly where it reached the sea floor
The sandstone formed deep in the crust under great heat and pressure from burial
The sandstone formed from wind-blown dust that settled in a dry, frozen desert
questions.explanation: Modern ripple marks form where water or wind moves loose sand. Matching ripples in the rock indicate a similar environment, such as a tidal flat or shallow sea. Lava and deep burial do not produce sand ripples.

questions.stem: A mudstone layer shows polygonal cracks filled with sand from the layer above. What does uniformitarianism suggest about the environment when the mud was deposited?
options: The mud was deposited in deep ocean water that never fell below its usual level
The mud was baked by a lava flow, which cracked it into hexagonal columns
The mud was frozen in a glacier and cracked as the glacier slid over rock
Wet mud was exposed to the air and dried out, as it does in drying puddles today
questions.explanation: Mud cracks form today when wet mud dries and shrinks, so the ancient cracks record a time when the mud was exposed and dried. Deep water would not let the mud dry out, and columnar jointing forms in cooling lava, not in mud.

questions.stem: Which observation shows a limitation of applying uniformitarianism strictly to Earth's whole history?
options: Waves today sort sand by grain size, as ancient beach sandstones show
Banded iron formations formed in oceans with almost no oxygen, conditions not found today
Rivers today deposit sand on their floodplains, as ancient rivers did in the past
Volcanoes today erupt lava that cools into basalt, as ancient basalts show
questions.explanation: Banded iron formations formed in oxygen-poor early oceans, a condition that does not exist now, so modern processes cannot fully explain them. The processes are the same kinds of chemistry and physics, but conditions and rates have changed. The other observations support uniformitarianism.

questions.stem: The law of superposition states that, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock:
options: The oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top
The thickest layer is the oldest and the thinnest is the youngest
The youngest layer is at the bottom and the oldest is at the top
The hardest layer is the oldest and the softest is the youngest
questions.explanation: Sediment is deposited on top of what is already there, so in an undisturbed sequence each layer is younger than the one beneath it. Layer thickness and hardness do not indicate relative age.

questions.stem: The principle of original horizontality states that:
options: Sediments are deposited in flat, horizontal layers, so tilted layers were disturbed later
All rock layers stay horizontal forever because Earth's crust does not move or fold
Horizontal layers are always younger than tilted layers found anywhere on Earth
Igneous intrusions always form horizontal sheets that run parallel to the bedding
questions.explanation: Gravity causes sediment to settle in nearly horizontal layers. If layers are now tilted or folded, they were deformed after they formed. The crust clearly can fold and tilt, which is how this principle is useful.

questions.stem: According to the principle of cross-cutting relationships, a fault or igneous dyke that cuts across rock layers is:
options: The same age as the layers it cuts
Older than the layer at the very top
Younger than the layers it cuts across
Older than the layers it cuts across
questions.explanation: A feature can only cut through rocks that already exist, so the fault or dyke must be younger than every layer it cuts. Layers that lie unbroken above it are younger than the fault or dyke.

questions.stem: The principle of inclusions states that fragments of one rock enclosed within another rock are:
options: Always made of the same mineral as the host
Older than the rock that encloses them
Younger than the rock that encloses them
Formed at the same time as the enclosing rock
questions.explanation: A fragment must already exist before it can be picked up and enclosed. Pebbles of granite in a conglomerate, or blocks of sandstone caught in a granite, are therefore older than the rock around them.

questions.stem: Sandstone layer P lies at the bottom of a cliff, with shale Q above it and limestone R at the top. A basalt dyke cuts through P and Q but stops at the base of R. What is the order of events, oldest first?
options: R, Q, dyke, P
P, Q, dyke, R
P, dyke, Q, R
Dyke, P, Q, R
questions.explanation: Superposition gives P, then Q, then R. The dyke cuts P and Q, so it is younger than both, but it does not cut R, so R was deposited after the dyke. The full order is P, Q, dyke, then R.

questions.stem: A granite contains angular blocks of a dark, fine-grained metamorphic rock. What does this show?
options: The metamorphic rock formed later, when the cooled granite was heated and squeezed
The granite and the metamorphic rock formed from the same magma at the same time
The metamorphic blocks were deposited on top of the granite by a later river
The metamorphic rock existed before the granite magma intruded and broke off pieces of it
questions.explanation: By the principle of inclusions, the blocks were already solid rock when the granite magma surrounded them, so the metamorphic rock is older. Blocks enclosed within the granite could not have been deposited on top of it.

questions.stem: A layer of basalt lies between two sedimentary layers. The sandstone below it shows baking at the contact, but the shale above shows no baking and contains pebbles of the basalt at its base. What is the best interpretation?
options: The basalt is younger than the shale, because it lies between the two layers
The basalt formed at the same time as both layers during a single eruption
The basalt is a lava flow that cooled at the surface before the shale was deposited on it
The basalt is a sill intruded between the two layers after both had been deposited
questions.explanation: A sill intruded later would bake the rocks both above and below it. Baking only below, plus basalt pebbles in the overlying shale, shows the lava cooled at the surface, was eroded, and was then covered by the shale. The basalt is therefore older than the shale.

questions.stem: Fossils in a thick sequence of rock layers always appear in the same vertical order, wherever the sequence is found. How is this fossil record used?
options: To show that all of the fossil species lived at exactly the same time
To prove that the layers were deposited at the same speed in every place
To put layers in relative order and match layers of the same age between sites
To give the exact age in years of each layer without any other evidence
questions.explanation: Because life changed through time, each layer holds a characteristic group of fossils, which lets geologists order layers and recognise layers of the same age in different places. Fossils alone give relative ages, not ages in years.

questions.stem: The same distinctive layer of volcanic ash is found in two outcrops 40 km apart. What is the most useful conclusion?
options: The rocks above the ash must be identical at both sites, because they were deposited together
The ash proves that both sites were once on the floor of the same deep ocean basin
The ash layer marks the same moment in time at both sites, so the two sequences can be correlated
The two outcrops were formed by two separate eruptions that happened millions of years apart
questions.explanation: An ash fall settles over a wide area almost instantly in geological terms, so it is an excellent marker bed for correlation. The rocks above it may differ between sites, because local environments can vary after the eruption.

questions.stem: At site 1, layer K (containing ammonite species A) lies above layer L (containing species B). At site 2, a layer with species B lies directly beneath a layer with species C, which is in turn beneath a layer with species A. What can be concluded?
options: Species A is older than species B, because it appears above it at both of the sites
Species C lived before species B, because its layer is found only at site 2
The two sites cannot be correlated, because they do not contain all the same layers
The species C layer at site 2 is missing at site 1, through erosion or non-deposition
questions.explanation: Both sites show B below A, so B is older. Site 2 has an extra layer with C between them, so that interval is missing at site 1, through erosion or because no sediment was deposited there. Correlation is still possible using the shared fossils.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a slow geological transition?
options: An earthquake displacing rock along a fault
A landslide covering a hillside road in mud
A mountain range being worn down by erosion
A volcanic eruption burying a valley in ash
questions.explanation: Erosion of a mountain range takes millions of years, so it is a slow transition. Eruptions, earthquakes and landslides change the land in minutes to days, so they are fast transitions.

questions.stem: Why is subduction classed as a slow geological transition, even though it can cause sudden earthquakes?
options: The sinking plate stops moving between earthquakes and only moves during each one
Subduction only occurs once, when a new ocean basin first opens between two continents
Subduction moves plates sideways but never downwards, so it changes the crust very little
The plate sinks only a few centimetres a year, so the process takes millions of years overall
questions.explanation: Plates move at a few centimetres a year, so subduction reshapes the crust over millions of years. Stress built up by this slow movement can be released suddenly as earthquakes, which are fast events within a slow process.

questions.stem: A sequence contains 40 m of fine shale, then a 2 m layer of coarse volcanic breccia with charred wood, then more shale. How should the breccia be interpreted?
options: A fast event, such as an eruption, interrupted slow deposition of mud
A slow event lasting much longer than the deposition of all of the shale
A period when mud deposition became faster but the setting did not change
A gap in time when no sediment of any kind was deposited at the site
questions.explanation: Fine shale builds up slowly from settling mud, while a thick breccia with charred wood records a sudden, violent event such as a volcanic eruption. The sequence shows slow deposition interrupted by a fast transition.

questions.stem: A conformable boundary between two rock layers indicates:
options: A long gap when older rocks were uplifted and eroded
Tilting of the lower layers before the upper ones formed
Intrusion of magma between the two layers after deposition
Continuous deposition with no significant break in time
questions.explanation: Conformable layers were deposited one after another without a significant time gap. An unconformity, by contrast, is an erosion surface or gap in deposition that represents missing time.

questions.stem: An unconformity is best described as:
options: A layer that contains more fossils than the layers above or below it
A buried erosion surface or gap that represents missing time in the rock record
A layer of rock that formed faster than the layers above and below it
A crack along which rocks on either side have moved past each other
questions.explanation: An unconformity is a surface where rock was eroded or deposition stopped before younger layers formed, so part of the time record is missing. A crack with movement is a fault, not an unconformity.

questions.stem: Steeply tilted layers of shale are cut off by an erosion surface and covered by flat-lying sandstone. What type of boundary is this?
options: A conformable boundary
A nonconformity
A disconformity
An angular unconformity
questions.explanation: An angular unconformity separates tilted or folded older layers from younger flat layers above. It records deposition, then tilting, then erosion, then renewed deposition. A disconformity has parallel layers on both sides, and a nonconformity has igneous or metamorphic rock below.

questions.stem: Horizontal sandstone lies directly on an eroded surface of granite. What type of boundary is this?
options: An angular unconformity
A disconformity
A conformable boundary
A nonconformity
questions.explanation: A nonconformity is an erosion surface with sedimentary rock lying on igneous or metamorphic rock. The granite formed deep underground, so it must have been uplifted and its cover eroded before the sand was deposited, representing a long gap in time.

questions.stem: In a sequence of parallel, flat-lying limestone layers, a surface is found where the lower layer has an uneven, eroded top with channels filled by sand from the layer above. What does this indicate?
options: An angular unconformity, because the lower layer was folded before erosion
A conformable boundary, because both layers are flat and parallel to each other
A fault, because the channels show that the two layers moved past each other
A disconformity, because deposition paused and erosion occurred without tilting
questions.explanation: Parallel layers separated by an erosion surface form a disconformity: the lower layer was exposed and eroded, then deposition resumed, but no tilting occurred. Because the layers are parallel, it is easy to mistake for a conformable boundary, but the eroded surface shows missing time.

questions.stem: Rock record: (1) layers A to C deposited; (2) layers tilted; (3) surface eroded; (4) layer D deposited flat on top; (5) a fault cuts A to D. Which statement is correct?
options: The tilting happened after the fault, because tilted rocks are always younger
The fault is the youngest event and the A-to-D boundary is an angular unconformity
The fault is older than layer D and the A-to-D boundary is a disconformity
Layer D is older than layers A to C, because it lies across the tilted layers
questions.explanation: The fault cuts all four layers, so by cross-cutting relationships it is the youngest event. Tilted layers overlain by flat ones across an erosion surface form an angular unconformity, not a disconformity, which has parallel layers.

questions.stem: Which combination of features makes a fossil a good index fossil?
options: Widespread, abundant, easily identified and lived for a short time
Rare, found in one place, hard to identify and lived for a long time
Widespread, rare, easily identified and lived for a very long time
Abundant, found in one place, easily identified and lived for a long time
questions.explanation: An index fossil must be widespread and abundant so it is found in many places, easy to recognise, and from a species that existed only briefly, so it pins rocks to a narrow time interval. A long-lived species could appear in rocks of very different ages.

questions.stem: Trilobites as a group lived for more than 250 million years, but individual trilobite species often lived for only a few million years. Which is the better index fossil?
options: Trilobites as a whole group, because they were found for a longer time
Neither, because fossils of animals with shells cannot be used for dating
Trilobites as a whole group, because more fossils of them are preserved
A single widespread trilobite species, because it narrows the age range
questions.explanation: An index fossil should have a short time range. A single species that lived for a few million years places rocks within a narrow window, whereas the whole group spans a huge interval and gives little precision.

questions.stem: Queensland geologist Dorothy Hill is recognised for which contribution to geology?
options: Measuring seismic waves to discover that Earth has a solid inner core inside a liquid outer core
Proposing continental drift after matching coastlines on opposite sides of the Atlantic
Dating meteorites to show that the age of Earth is about 4.54 billion years
Using fossil corals to correlate Palaeozoic rocks and refine geological maps of Queensland
questions.explanation: Dorothy Hill studied fossil corals and showed how they could be used to correlate Palaeozoic rocks, which improved stratigraphy and the geological mapping of Queensland. She became the first woman to hold a professorship at an Australian university, at the University of Queensland.

questions.stem: The boundaries between many major divisions of the geological timescale, such as the end of the Palaeozoic and the end of the Mesozoic, were placed where:
options: The thickest rock layers in a sequence end and thinner ones begin
The fossil record shows major changes, such as mass extinctions
Rock layers change from sedimentary to igneous across the world
Radiometric dates fall on exact multiples of 100 million years
questions.explanation: The geological timescale was first built from relative ages, with boundaries placed at major changes in fossils. The end of the Palaeozoic marks the Permian mass extinction and the end of the Mesozoic marks the Cretaceous mass extinction. Radiometric dating later added ages in years.

questions.stem: Which list places the three eras of the Phanerozoic Eon in order from oldest to youngest?
options: Palaeozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic
Mesozoic, Palaeozoic, Cenozoic
Cenozoic, Mesozoic, Palaeozoic
Palaeozoic, Cenozoic, Mesozoic
questions.explanation: The Palaeozoic ('ancient life') came first, then the Mesozoic ('middle life'), then the Cenozoic ('recent life'), in which we live now. The names reflect the fossils characteristic of each era.

questions.stem: How do index fossils and stratigraphic evidence together build the geological timescale?
options: Stratigraphy orders the layers, and index fossils match layers of the same age between regions
Index fossils give the exact age in years, and stratigraphy shows where the fossils lived
Stratigraphy measures the decay of isotopes, and index fossils record the temperature
Index fossils show the rock type, and stratigraphy gives the age of each fossil in years
questions.explanation: Superposition and the other principles order rocks within one place, and index fossils allow layers in different regions to be matched, building a global relative sequence. Ages in years come from radiometric dating, not from fossils or stratigraphy alone.

questions.stem: The half-life of a radioisotope is:
options: Half of the time taken for all of the parent atoms to decay
The time taken for a mineral to lose half of its total mass
The time taken for the daughter atoms to decay back to the parent
The time taken for half of the parent atoms in a sample to decay
questions.explanation: A half-life is the time for half of the remaining parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms. Decay never quite reaches zero, so 'half the time to decay completely' has no meaning, and daughter atoms do not turn back into parent atoms.

questions.stem: A mineral originally contained only parent isotope. It now contains 25% parent isotope and 75% daughter isotope. If the half-life is 1.25 billion years, how old is the mineral?
options: 3.75 billion years
0.94 billion years
2.5 billion years
1.25 billion years
questions.explanation: After one half-life 50% of the parent remains, and after two half-lives 25% remains. Two half-lives of 1.25 billion years give 2.5 billion years. Choosing 3.75 billion years treats the 75% daughter as three half-lives.

questions.stem: A rock sample has a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1 : 7. How many half-lives have passed since it formed, assuming it began with no daughter isotope?
questions.explanation: A ratio of 1 : 7 means the parent is 1/8 of the original atoms. Half remains after one half-life, a quarter after two and an eighth after three, so three half-lives have passed. Seven and eight confuse the ratio with the number of half-lives.

questions.stem: A half-life graph plots the percentage of parent isotope remaining against time. What shape is the curve?
options: A straight line falling at a constant rate until it reaches zero at two half-lives
A curve that rises steeply at first and then levels off at one hundred per cent
A straight horizontal line, because the amount of parent isotope does not change
A curve that falls steeply at first and then levels off, halving in each equal time interval
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is exponential: in each half-life the parent falls by half of what remains, so the curve drops steeply then flattens, approaching zero. A straight line would mean the same number of atoms decayed in every interval.

questions.stem: A half-life graph for an isotope shows 100% parent at time 0 and 50% at 700 million years. A zircon contains 12.5% of its original parent. Read from the pattern, how old is the zircon?
options: 1400 million years
5600 million years
875 million years
2100 million years
questions.explanation: The graph shows a half-life of 700 million years. 12.5% is one eighth, which is three half-lives (100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5), so the age is 3 × 700 = 2100 million years. Choosing 1400 million years stops at two half-lives.

questions.stem: Why is radiometric dating most often applied to igneous rocks rather than sedimentary rocks?
options: Igneous rocks decay much faster than sedimentary rocks, so their ages are easier to measure
Sedimentary rocks are always younger than one thousand years, so they are too young to date
Igneous minerals start their clocks on crystallising, but sediment grains predate the rock
Sedimentary rocks contain no radioactive isotopes at all, so there is nothing for them to measure
questions.explanation: When magma crystallises, new minerals trap parent isotopes with no daughter, so the clock starts at formation. Grains in a sedimentary rock were eroded from older rocks, so dating them gives the age of the source rock, not when the sediment was deposited.

questions.stem: A sandstone layer lies above a lava flow dated at 180 million years and below a volcanic ash bed dated at 150 million years. What can be said about the sandstone's age?
options: It is older than 180 million years
It is younger than 150 million years
It is between 150 and 180 million years old
It is exactly 165 million years old
questions.explanation: By superposition the sandstone is younger than the lava below it and older than the ash above it, so its age is bracketed between 150 and 180 million years. Assuming it is exactly halfway is not justified, because deposition rates are unknown.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5730 years, unsuitable for dating a 300-million-year-old granite?
options: Carbon-14 only forms inside igneous rocks after they have been exposed at the surface
Carbon-14 half-life is too long, so too little of it would have decayed to measure
Almost no carbon-14 would remain after so many half-lives, and granite contains little carbon
Carbon-14 decays faster in hot rocks, so its half-life inside granite is not known
questions.explanation: After tens of thousands of years so little carbon-14 is left that it cannot be measured, and granite is not formed from living material. Isotopes with very long half-lives, such as uranium-238, are used for old rocks. Decay rates are not affected by temperature.

questions.stem: The accepted age of Earth, about 4.54 billion years, was calculated mainly by radiometric dating of meteorites. Why are meteorites used rather than Earth's oldest rocks?
options: Earth's oldest rocks have never been found or dated, so meteorites are the only rocks that can be measured
Meteorites formed long before the solar system existed, so they show when the first stars formed
Earth's first rocks were recycled by plate movement and erosion; meteorites stayed unaltered
Meteorites contain much more uranium than Earth rocks, so they decay faster and are easier to measure
questions.explanation: Earth's earliest crust has been destroyed by subduction, melting and erosion, so no rocks survive from its formation. Meteorites formed at the same time as the solar system and have not been reprocessed, so they record its age, which is consistent with younger ages from Earth and Moon rocks.

questions.stem: How did the discovery of radioactivity change geology?
options: It replaced fossils entirely, so index fossils are no longer used by geologists
It proved that Earth is only a few million years old, much younger than once thought
It let numerical ages be added to a timescale previously built from relative ages
It showed that the principle of superposition was wrong and should no longer be used
questions.explanation: Before radioactivity was understood, geologists could only order events. Radioactive decay provided a clock to give ages in years, which were added to the existing relative timescale. Superposition and index fossils are still used together with radiometric dates.
